Elon Musk’s X Corp claimed platforms should not be responsible for protecting children from “violent pornography” or “content that promotes seriously harmful behaviour”, an Australian government official has claimed.

The social media company responded to a government survey in 2025 consulting on potential legislation which would shift platform duty of care from reactive complaint responses to active risk management.

When asked what kinds of harmful experiences or material digital platforms should take steps to prevent for Australians under 18, an officer for X Corp ticked “none of the above”.

The survey listed multiple forms of inappropriate online material including “hate speech”, “violent pornography” and “content that promotes seriously harmful behaviour”.

First assistant secretary of the government’s digital platforms, safety and classification division Sarah Vandenbroek provided evidence of X’s response during the Royal Commission on anti-Semitism and Social Cohesion on Friday.

Ms Vandenbroek said the company’s reply was “disappointing” and she was “not aware” of similar responses from any other social media platform.

The commission also heard the Australian government had been continually delayed with implementing the proactive duty of care into Australian legislation.

Proposed changes were clarified in the Rickard Review in 2024 yet are unlikely to be legislated within the next twelve months, according to Ms Vandenbroek.

The in-depth report collated opinions from 2200 Australians about the effectiveness of the Online Safety Act in protecting people, ultimately outlining 67 recommendations for change.

The royal commission heard it took the government 18 months to provide an incomplete response to the report.

Ms Vandenbroek acknowledged that period was “a long time”, yet defended the process on Friday.

The first assistant secretary cited issues with the changeover of ministers, the priority of implementing the under 16s social media ban and the workload involved in analysing the number of recommendations.

She blamed delays on the “complexity” of the process, rather than the team of up to nine people responsible for coping with the “extensive” workload.

“There was a process of briefing the new minister and the new office on the review so a lot of the work that was done … was then redone,” Ms Vandenbroek told the commission.

“And then it was the availability of various stakeholders and legal advice.”

Anthropic protects users

Anthropic’s approach to online safety contrasted to X Corp’s denial of a duty of care.

With thorough AI training modules to regulate and shut down hate speech, the AI company said it prioritised user safety.

Anthropic’s Australian and New Zealand general manager Theo Hourmouzis told the commission a test of 50,000 chats on their AI model, Claude, was conducted to analyse the presence of anti-Semitism.

Mr Hourmouzis revealed there was an “extraordinarily low return rate” of five instances identified as negatively targeting Jewish faith.

The general manager referred to the nature of the platform which engages users in one-on-one conversation with a chatbot, as well as sophisticated AI training, to explain such low levels.

“We’ve spent a lot of time on ensuring the policies are reviewed to get as close to zero as possible,” Mr Hourmouzis told the commission.

Anthropic reviews conversations and will “off-board” users for anti-Semitic views if necessary.

Using a three strike based system, safeguards escalate instances from simplifying redirecting conversation to more severe circumstances which result in the engagement of law enforcement.

The commission was set up in the wake of the Bondi Beach terror attack in Sydney’s east that killed 15 innocent people who were celebrating Chanukah on December 14.

The commission’s final report is due to be handed down in December, a year on from the Bondi attack.

Originally published as Elon Musk’s X Corp claims no duty to protect children from violent pornography
